enEdits.find: GPS systems must calibrate for both special relativity effects (satellites move fast, so clocks run slow by about 7 μs/day) and general relativity effects (being further from Earth, the gravitational field is weaker, so clocks run fast by about 45 μs/day). enEdits.replace: The GPS system has to correct for both effects. The satellites move fast, so their atomic clocks run slow by about 7 μs/day (special relativity); being far from Earth, where gravity is weaker, they run fast by about 45 μs/day (general relativity). Net: the satellite clocks run fast relative to ground clocks by about 38 μs/day, and that is the amount that has to be corrected. Ashby (2003) gives a nominal fractional frequency offset of 4.4647 × 10⁻¹⁰, i.e. ≈ 38.6 μs/day — consistent with the 38 μs figure. The 7 / 45 μs split above is the standard presentation in teaching materials (Pogge, Ohio State); it is not how Ashby breaks it down, since he works directly with the frequency offset. Ignoring that 38 μs/day would build up a timing error equivalent to about 11 km of light-travel distance every day — enough to make the system useless.
